'''Kyalami Grand Prix Circuit''' (from ''Khaya lami'', ''My home'' in [[Zulu language|Zulu]]) is a {{cvt|4.529|km|mi|abbr=on}} motor racing circuit located in [[Midrand]], [[Gauteng]], [[South Africa]], just north of [[Johannesburg]]. The name '''Kyalami''' also commonly refers to the suburb where the race track is located. The circuit has been used for [[Grand Prix motor racing|Grand Prix]] and [[Formula One]] races and has hosted the [[South African Grand Prix]] twenty times. Among the [[Formula One]] races held at the track the [[1977 South African Grand Prix]] stands out, as it is principally remembered for the fatal accident that claimed the lives of race marshal Frederick Jansen van Vuuren and driver [[Tom Pryce]]. In recent years, the area surrounding the circuit has developed into a residential and commercial suburb of [[Johannesburg]]. More recently, Kyalami has played host to five rounds of the [[Superbike World Championship]] from 1998 to 2002 and later in 2009 and 2010, the season finale of the [[Superstars Series]] in 2009 and 2010, and the South African round of the [[2008–09 A1 Grand Prix season]]. International racing returned to the circuit in November 2019, when it hosted the [[2019 Kyalami 9 Hours]], serving as the season finale of the [[2019 Intercontinental GT Challenge]].

== History ==
The original, sweeping circuit was designed and cleared by Harry Pierce and Dick Bremner along with a few friends and workers in the mid-1950s. The two were also responsible for the hosting and housing of early race teams that ventured to Africa to try out the new track with Bremner being the chairman of the South African Automotive Racing Association. The circuit was opened on 4 November 1961 with the race of [[Kyalami 9 Hours]].<ref name='kyalami_circuit_facts'>{{cite web |title=Kyalami - Circuit Facts |url=http://kyalamigrandprixcircuit.com/pebble.asp?relid=260 |website=Kyalami Grand Prix Circuit |access-date=1 December 2019}}</ref><ref name='kyalami_circuit_history'>{{cite web |title=Kyalami - Circuit History |url=https://kyalamigrandprixcircuit.com/pebble.asp?relid=264 |website=Kyalami Grand Prix Circuit |access-date=20 April 2025}}</ref> Its first major international event was in [[1961 Rand Grand Prix|1961]] until political sanctions (due to [[apartheid]] policies) eliminated the [[List of Formula One Grands Prix|Grand Prix]] after the [[1985 South African Grand Prix|1985 race]].<ref>{{cite web |last= |first= |title=Kyalami |url=http://www.grandprix.com/gpe/cir-069.html |website=grandprix.com}}</ref> The final race at the original circuit was held on 26 November 1988.<ref name='kyalami_circuit_history' />

===Original layout: 1961–1988===
[[File:Kyalami 1968layout.svg|thumb|left|Original layout of Kyalami]]

The clockwise track layout was based on a long straight with nine corners that had their naming inspired by a mix of local geography, South African cultural elements, and racing terminology. A lap started in close to the pit lane entrance on the '''Main Straight''' - a straight that lead downhill into the first bend.<ref name='kyalami_circuit_history' />
# '''Crowthorne Corner''' – A tight right-hander, being the first turn after the start-finish straight.  The corner was named after the [[Crowthorne, Gauteng|Crowthorne Hotel]], located near this particular section of the circuit.
# '''Barbecue Bend''' A second right-hand medium speed bend likely named after the tradition of South African [[Regional variations of barbecue#Africa|barbecues (braais)]], which were often held near this section of the track during race events.
# '''Jukskei Sweep''' This was a long, fast left-hand curve, named for the [[Jukskei River]], which runs near the track. The river itself is named after the traditional Afrikaner game of [[Jukskei]] (similar to horse-shoes), which was played by early settlers.{{cn|date=April 2026}}
# '''Sunset Bend''' A fast right-hander considered one of the iconic corners on the track. It was so named because the corner often forced drives to face the setting sun while navigating this section of the track.
# '''Clubhouse Bend'''  A 90-degree left-hander named after the motorsport clubhouse that was located at this bend on the track.
# '''Esses 1''' Bend one:  initial left-hander.
# '''Esses 2'''. Right-handed 90-degree bend, leading to steep uphill into turn 8.
# '''Leeukop Bend''' Leeukop was a tight right-hand hairpin that led onto the initial part of the long straight.  This corner was named after Leeukop hill (Lion's Head), a common and prominent geographical naming feature in South African topography.  It also referred to the [[Leeukop Prison]] that was located behind the hill on adjacent land.
# '''The Kink''' This was a right deviation in the track splitting the main straight into two sections.

===Revised layout: 1989 to present===
When the circuit was rebuilt in 1989 as part of a commercial development, Leeukop Bend, the Kink, Pit lane, the start/finish straight, Crowthorne Corner and Barbecue Bend were all eliminated.<ref name='kyalami_circuit_history' /> Jukskei Sweep was heavily modified to create the entrance into the bend before the then newly built Pit lane and start/finish straight. The remaining part of the old fast circuit, modified to a lesser degree were Sunset Bend, Clubhouse Bend and the Esses still incorporated into the current configuration, with the result that the circuit became a narrow, twisty ribbon rather than one of the fastest circuits on the calendar. Formula One abandoned the rebuilt circuit in [[1993 Formula One season|1993]] after just two races on the new layout, caused by a bankruptcy on the part of the promoter.

It hosted the [[South African motorcycle Grand Prix]] until 1992.

Kyalami was changed again with the building of the current pit lane and start/finish straight and later again changes were made, with the addition of a chicane which in turn was removed again for the 2009 World Superbike race.<ref name='kyalami_circuit_history' /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gdecarli.it/php/circuit.php?var1=713&var2=2|title=TRACKS: KYALAMI|first=Guido|last=de Carli|website=gdecarli.it|access-date=24 May 2012|archive-date=3 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303225703/http://www.gdecarli.it/php/circuit.php?var1=713&var2=2|url-status=dead}}</ref> Kyalami came under new management and 2008 saw the 50th anniversary of the 9-hour revival being held at Kyalami with golden oldies like [[David Piper (racing driver)|David Piper]] and others.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.motoring.co.za/index.php?fArticleId=4722182|title=THREE-HOUR ENDURANCE RACE FOR HISTORIC CARS|date=20 November 2008|publisher=[[Independent Online (South Africa)|Independent Online]]|access-date=23 February 2009}}</ref> On 6 June 2014, it was announced that Kyalami would be auctioned off on 24 July without reserve.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.enca.com/kyalami-race-track-goes-under-hammer|title=Kyalami race track to go under the hammer|first=Bianca|last=Ackroyd|website=enca.com|access-date=11 June 2014|archive-date=6 October 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221006132144/https://www.enca.com/kyalami-race-track-goes-under-hammer|url-status=dead}}</ref> On 24 July 2014, it was auctioned off for R205&nbsp;million. The winning bidder was [[Toby Venter]], owner of [[Porsche|Porsche South Africa]].<ref name='kyalami_circuit_history' /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.timeslive.co.za/local/2014/07/24/kyalami-race-track-auctioned-for-r205-million-in-under-two-minutes|title=TimesLIVE|website=Sunday Times (Johannesburg)|access-date=25 July 2014|archive-date=1 January 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180101030646/http://www.timeslive.co.za/local/2014/07/24/kyalami-race-track-auctioned-for-r205-million-in-under-two-minutes|url-status=dead}}</ref> R100 million was invested to upgrade the circuit, allowing it to successfully obtain an [[FIA]] Grade 2 status.<ref name='kyalami_rcircuits'>{{cite web |title=Kyalami - Racing Circuits |url=https://www.racingcircuits.info/africa/south-africa/kyalami.html |website=RacingCircuits.info |access-date=11 December 2019}}</ref>

On 12 December 2019, the provisional calendar for the [[2020–21 FIA World Endurance Championship]] was announced, containing a six-hour race at Kyalami scheduled for 6 February 2021.<ref name="prov cal">{{cite web |title=Monza and Kyalami on 2020–2021 WEC calendar |url=https://www.grandprix247.com/2019/12/12/monza-and-kyalami-on-2020-2021-wec-calendar/ |website=GrandPrix247 |date=12 December 2019 |access-date=12 December 2019}}</ref> However, after the calendar was revised due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], Kyalami was removed.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.motorsport.com/wec/news/2021-calendar-abandons-winter-format/4776572/|title=WEC shelves winter calendar format for 2021|website=www.motorsport.com|language=en|access-date=19 March 2021}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=2021 FIA WEC provisional calendar revealed|url=https://www.fiawec.com/en/news/2021-fia-wec-provisional-calendar-revealed/6859|access-date=19 March 2021|website=www.fiawec.com|language=en}}</ref>

==South African Grand Prix==
From [[1967 Formula One Season|1967]] to [[1993 Formula One Season|1993]], Kyalami hosted 21 editions of the South African Grand Prix. Perhaps the most infamous of these was the [[1982 South African Grand Prix|1982 edition]], when the [[Grand Prix Drivers' Association]] staged a [[Strike action|strike]] in protest of new [[superlicence]] conditions imposed by [[Fédération Internationale du Sport Automobile|FISA]].

[[Niki Lauda]] became the most successful driver at Kyalami, taking his third victory at the circuit in [[1984 South African Grand Prix|1984]]. [[Alain Prost]], [[Nigel Mansell]] and [[Jackie Stewart]] are the joint second-most successful drivers at the circuit, with two wins each. [[Jody Scheckter]] became the first and only South African driver to win their home race during the [[1975 South African Grand Prix|1975 edition]]. [[Scuderia Ferrari|Ferrari]] and [[Williams Grand Prix Engineering|Williams]] are the most successful constructors at the circuit, with four wins each.

In June 2022 it was reported that [[Stefano Domenicali]], the President of Formula One, had flown to South Africa to meet representatives of the circuit about a possible return for F1 in 2023, but the course was not included in the 2023 provisional calendar.<ref>{{Cite news |title=F1 closes in on deal for South African GP |url=https://www.bbc.com/sport/formula1/61786715 |language=en-GB |work=BBC Sport |access-date=13 June 2022}}</ref>
